hints: Look closely at what the scale bar tells you. It says 2 μm, so that printed line represents a real length of 2 μm in life, but how long does it look on the paper?
Remember magnification = image size divided by actual size. How could you get magnification using just the scale bar line, without even measuring the cell?
walkthrough:
**Recall what magnification really means**

Think of magnification as how many times bigger the picture is than real life.

Key rule:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$
Both sizes must be in the same units.

**Use the scale bar as your image**

The scale bar has an actual size of $2 \, \mu m$. Its image size is how long you measure it on the page with a ruler.

So first measure that line in millimetres, then convert to micrometres:
$$1 \, \text{mm} = 1000 \, \mu m$$

**Divide to get magnification**

Now divide the measured image length (in $\mu m$) by the true length ($2 \, \mu m$).
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{scale bar image length in } \mu m}{2 \, \mu m}$$
That is exactly the method described in option C.

options.A: This only compares the cell to the scale bar on paper. It does not use the real 2 μm value, so it cannot give magnification.
options.B: This mixes up the cell measurement and the conversion. Multiplying by 2000 and dividing by the scale bar length does not follow image divided by actual.
options.C: Correct. The measured scale bar length converted to μm is the image size, and 2 μm is the actual size, so image divided by 2 gives magnification.
options.D: This correctly converts units but then multiplies by 2 instead of dividing. Magnification needs image divided by actual, so you must divide by 2.
